chapter.name: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral
chapter.blurb: Acidic, basic and neutral substances, litmus, natural and turmeric indicators, olfactory indicators and neutralisation in daily life.

scope: Litmus and acidic, basic, neutral substances

concepts.name: Acidic, basic and neutral substances: litmus as an indicator
concepts.description: Testing substances with litmus paper, grouping them as acidic, basic or neutral, and taste and feel of acids and bases.
concepts.idea: Litmus shows different colours in acids and bases and so classifies substances as acidic, basic or neutral.
concepts.rule: Litmus is a natural substance from lichens, available as a solution and as red and blue litmus paper. Substances that turn blue litmus red are acidic; those that turn red litmus blue are basic; those that change neither are neutral. Because litmus shows different colours in acidic and basic solutions it is an acid-base indicator. Lemon juice, amla juice, tamarind water and vinegar are acidic; soap solution, baking soda solution, lime water and washing powder solution are basic; tap water, sugar solution and salt solution are neutral. Acids taste sour and bases generally taste bitter and feel soapy or slippery, though bitter gourd is bitter but not basic. Never taste unknown substances. Lime water is calcium hydroxide in water, made by mixing chuna (calcium oxide) in water. Lichens are a fungus and an alga living together.
concepts.example: Baking soda solution feels soapy or slippery.

concepts.name: Natural indicators: red rose and other plants
concepts.description: Preparing a red rose extract, its colours in acids and bases, other natural indicators and hydrangea.
concepts.idea: Plant extracts like red rose, purple cabbage and beetroot can act as natural acid-base indicators.
concepts.rule: To prepare a red rose extract, collect fallen petals, wash and crush them, place them in a tumbler, pour hot water (under adult supervision), cover for 5 to 10 minutes and filter. The red rose extract gives red in acidic solutions and green in basic solutions and does not change in neutral ones, just as litmus does. Beetroot, purple cabbage, turmeric, jamun and red hibiscus can also act as indicators. Hydrangea flowers are blue in acidic soil and pink or red in basic soil, so gardeners may change their colour by changing the soil's nature. Do not pluck flowers; use fallen petals.
concepts.example: Hydrangea grows in the Himalayan region and the north-eastern states.

concepts.name: Turmeric paper and olfactory indicators
concepts.description: Making turmeric paper, its behaviour with acids, bases and neutral substances, and indicators that use smell.
concepts.idea: Turmeric paper turns red only in bases, and olfactory indicators change smell in acids or bases.
concepts.rule: Turmeric paper is made by dipping filter paper in a paste of turmeric (haldi) in water, drying it and cutting it into strips. It turns red in basic solutions and stays yellow in acidic and neutral ones, so it can test bases but cannot tell acids from neutral substances. Turmeric is called a golden spice and is a member of the ginger family. A curry stain turns red on applying soap for this reason. Ashwin wrote a message on turmeric-coated paper using a basic solution. Substances whose odours change in acidic or basic media are olfactory indicators, such as finely chopped onion whose smell disappears with baking soda and stays with tamarind water.
concepts.example: A curry stain on a white shirt changes colour when soap is applied.

concepts.name: Neutralisation reactions
concepts.description: What happens when an acid mixes with a base, the equation for neutralisation, and Acharya P.C. Ray.
concepts.idea: An acid and a base react to form salt and water and release heat.
concepts.rule: When lime water is added slowly to lemon juice solution with blue litmus, the colour changes from red to blue, showing that the solution is no longer acidic; lime water has neutralised the acid. When an acid solution is mixed with a base in sufficient quantity the result is neither acidic nor basic. Such reactions are neutralisation reactions. In a neutralisation reaction salt and water are formed with the release of heat: acid + base gives salt + water + heat. Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray, the 'Father of Modern Indian Chemistry', set up India's first pharmaceutical company in 1901, wrote on the history of chemistry in India and advocated the mother tongue as the medium of instruction.
concepts.example: Adding one more drop of lemon juice after neutralisation turns litmus red again.

concepts.name: Neutralisation in daily life
concepts.description: Ant bites and baking soda, treating acidic and basic soil, and neutralising acidic factory waste.
concepts.idea: Neutralisation helps treat ant bites, soil and factory waste.
concepts.rule: When a red ant bites it injects an acidic liquid, formic acid; rubbing moist baking soda, a base, neutralises the acid and relieves pain. Excess use of chemical fertilisers can make soil acidic so plants grow poorly; acidic soil is treated with lime, a base. If soil is basic, organic matter like manure and composted leaves is added because it releases acids that neutralise it. Sometimes soil is neutral but plants are unhealthy due to nutrient deficiency. If acidic waste from factories is released into a lake, fish decline; the waste can be neutralised by adding basic substances before release.
concepts.example: Factory waste is neutralised before it is released into lakes.
